lines: A population of K·m items carries unknown values θᵢ in K groups, each group g with an unknown common offset b_g. Under a unit budget the experimenter must return a threshold set — which items lie above a fixed level. The values are not the goal; the answer is. Two measurements are available, and the distinction between them is the whole subject. An ORDINARY query on item i returns θᵢ + b_g(i) with variance v at unit price, seeing value and offset only in combination. A CALIBRATION query on group g returns b_g directly, with variance ν, at price κ. The dilemma is concrete: calibration consumes budget that could have bought ordinary samples. If it merely improves efficiency, a careful allocator trades it off and the question is tuning. If instead some configurations admit no answer from ordinary sampling at all, the trade-off framing is wrong — calibration is a precondition, and an allocator economising on it fails outright rather than gracefully. Two questions, and no others: WHEN does the calibration query become mandatory, and WHAT does it cost exactly?

C1.  NECESSITY, WITH AN EXACT WITNESS. Two worlds, in exact rationals, that every ordinary query cannot tell apart while their answers differ. The attainable value there is exactly zero, so calibration is a precondition rather than an option. C2.  THE EXACT PRICE OF ONE UNIT. A group delivering profiled information h costs at least h(√m + √κ)², and the attaining split is exhibited. The two prices combine through their SQUARE ROOTS, and the constant is exact. C3.  THE PRICE LAW, MATCHED AND ATTAINED. Γ* = Δ²/(2K(√m+√κ)²), proved over EVERY unit-budget design rather than a parametric family, with a design meeting it. It yields the operational crossover κ = m. C4.  OMITTING THE QUERY IS STRICTLY WORSE. On one explicit instance every anchor-free design is capped at 1/8 — attained, hence tight — against 261/1520 anchored, a gap of 37.4%. C5.  MACHINE-CHECKED. Four Lean 4 modules, 29 audited declarations, no sorry, axioms confined to {propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound}.
The argument is a chain of eight steps. Each states what is proved, how it was closed, and how it depends on the step before.
Four items, two per group, are exhibited together with a second world reached by shifting one group and paying the shift back through its offset:

Item 0 lies above threshold in the first world and below it in the second, while item 3 lies above in both — yet every ordinary query has an identical mean in the two worlds. The attainable value is exactly zero, not merely small.
WHY THIS FOLLOWS FROM STEP 1. Step 1 shows the offset must be measured. Step 2 asks what a measurement of it is worth, by eliminating the offset from the energy:
Fig. 1.  The price law against a realised error rate. 240 random instances, spanning eight group counts and a thirtyfold range of separation, collapse onto the predicted curve.
STEP 5 — THE K-GROUP UPPER BOUND  (contribution C3).
WHY THIS FOLLOWS FROM STEP 4. Step 4 prices one group; Step 5 sums that price across K groups and confronts it with the unit budget, converting a per-group cost into a cap on the whole design.

Free calibration recovers the cost of the ordinary queries alone; expensive calibration dominates the budget; at the crossover κ = m the two square roots are equal and each query type consumes exactly half of each group's budget.
STEP 7 — THE ANCHOR IS MANDATORY  (contribution C4).

WHY THIS FOLLOWS FROM STEP 6. Step 6 prices a design that already includes the calibration query; Step 7 asks whether omitting it can ever be competitive, on one instance where both sides are computable exactly.

THE LAW IS EXACT, AND INDEPENDENT NUMERICS AGREE. Bisection and Nelder–Mead over the same feasible set, 32 cells: largest relative gap 2.5×10⁻¹⁶, and neither ever exceeds the closed form — the direction that would falsify an upper bound. REMOVING THE CONTROL QUERY GIVES EXACTLY ZERO on all 32 cells. BAD ALLOCATION COSTS A BOUNDED FRACTION: a uniform design keeping all controls reaches 73.5–100% of the optimum, median 91.7%. THE LAW PREDICTS A REALISED ERROR, not only a design value: over 240 random instances the error of a plug-in profiled test collapses onto Φ(−√(Γ*B)) with rms 0.006.
Fig. 2.  What each broken assumption costs. Misspecifying the noise shape is nearly free; a wrong separation, or contaminated anchors, costs an order of magnitude more.

The two results are asymmetric, and that is the practical message. Allocating badly loses a bounded fraction of the attainable information; omitting the query TYPE loses everything, and no amount of sampling recovers it. Efficiency and feasibility are not points on one scale, and a procedure treating calibration as one more option cannot detect the failure. The crossover κ = m gives the rule: below it calibration is cheap insurance, above it calibration is the binding cost and the group size m is what must be reconsidered. SCOPE. The law assumes common v, ν, κ and equal gaps; heterogeneous cases are measured but not proved. Step 7 certifies ONE instance — anchor-free designs CAN be beaten, not that they always are. Step 1 exhibits two indistinguishable worlds without characterising all of them. Everything is an information and budget statement: no estimator and no finite-sample guarantee is claimed.

A calibration query is not an efficiency improvement a careful allocator could do without. On the configurations exhibited here the attainable value is exactly zero until a query of the new type is bought; once bought, its price is exact — matched by a lower bound, an upper bound over all unit-budget designs, and an attaining design.
